opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is in terms of where the computation actually happens. With chain-of-thought, the model does its extra thinking by writing things down. It produces tokens, those tokens get fed back in, and every intermediate step has to be squeezed through this very narrow bottleneck of picking one discrete word out of the vocabulary. That has real advantages. You can read it, at least in principle, and it piggybacks on all the reasoning patterns that are already present in human text. But it's also a bit of a strange constraint when you think about it. The model has this very rich, high-dimensional internal state, and at every step we force it to collapse that into a single token and then reconstruct everything from there.

Latent reasoning is the idea that the model can do more of that thinking internally, in its continuous hidden state, without having to verbalize every step. In our work on recurrent-depth models, the concrete version is that you have a block of layers that you can loop over again and again at test time. So instead of spending more compute by generating more tokens, you spend more compute by iterating deeper on the same token, refining the representation in latent space. The model can, in a sense, think longer before it says anything at all.

And I don't think of these as strict competitors. They're two different axes of scaling test-time compute. Some things are probably very naturally expressed in language, like when you need to lay out a plan or keep track of a long sequence of facts. But there are other kinds of reasoning, spatial intuition, some kinds of search, maybe things that are just hard to put into words, where forcing everything through text is pretty inefficient. People do a lot of reasoning that never turns into an inner monologue. So the hope with latent reasoning is that you capture that kind of computation as well, and that you don't need specialized chain-of-thought training data for it to emerge. You just give the model the capacity to recur, and it learns to use it.

The obvious trade-off is interpretability. With chain-of-thought you get this readable trace, even if it's not always faithful to what the model is actually doing. With latent reasoning you lose that, so you have to develop new tools to look inside and understand what those iterations are actually computing. I think that's one of the really interesting open questions here.

r001.rationale: The response describes internal, continuous hidden-state computation and refining representations before verbalizing, but does not clearly characterize this as learning algorithms in that representation space.

r002.rationale: It says chain-of-thought does extra thinking by writing tokens that are fed back in, and that it draws on reasoning patterns in human text—clearly framing reasoning as scaffolded onto language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that chain-of-thought is reasoning that's forced to pass through the token bottleneck. Every step the model takes has to be verbalized, sampled into a discrete token, and then fed back in. So you get this very legible trace, which is great, but it's also a huge constraint. You're asking the model to compress whatever it's computing internally into a vocabulary of, say, a hundred thousand symbols, one at a time, and then re-expand it on the next forward pass.

Latent reasoning is the idea that you let the model keep iterating in its own representation space instead. So you take the hidden state, you run it through some block again, and again, and you don't collapse it to a token in between. There's nothing to read off, but the model also isn't losing information at every step. It can represent things that don't have a clean linguistic description, hold multiple hypotheses in superposition, do something closer to continuous optimization rather than symbolic search.

The analogy I like is that chain-of-thought is sort of like thinking out loud, and latent reasoning is more like the stuff you do before you even know what you'd say. Humans do both, and I think models probably should too. A lot of what we'd call intuition or pattern completion doesn't naturally decompose into verbal steps, and if you force it to, you're spending a lot of tokens on something that could be a few extra passes through the network.

Where it gets interesting is the trade-off. Chain-of-thought gives you interpretability for free, and it gives you a natural way to scale compute at test time, because you just generate more tokens. With latent reasoning you have to build that scaling in architecturally, something like a recurrent block you can unroll for as many steps as the problem needs. That's what we were going after with the depth-recurrent models: can you train something where the amount of computation per token is a knob you turn at inference, without the model ever having to write anything down. And then the honest open question is whether you lose something important when you take away the language, both in terms of oversight and in terms of whether language itself is doing useful work as a scaffold for the computation. My view is you want both, and the real question is how they should compose.

r001.rationale: The response says latent reasoning iterates in representation space without converting each step into a token, but it does not characterize this as learning algorithms there before decoding into language.

r002.rationale: It describes chain-of-thought as verbalizing each reasoning step into a discrete token and feeding it back, which communicates reasoning scaffolded onto language.

astra-6.text:
I think the main distinction is where the intermediate computation happens. With language-based chain of thought, the model writes out intermediate steps as tokens. Those tokens become part of its context, and it can use them to arrive at an answer. So language is both the way it communicates and a kind of scratchpad.

With latent reasoning, the idea is to do that intermediate work in the model’s internal representations, without having to turn every step into a word. You could imagine updating a hidden state repeatedly, giving the model more computation before it produces an answer.

But I’d be careful about making this a binary distinction. A model generating a chain of thought is already doing computation in its hidden states. The visible text isn’t necessarily a complete account of that computation. The question is really: do we require the intermediate steps to pass through discrete language tokens, or can we carry information forward in a continuous representation?

Language gives you a very useful structure, and it gives us something we can inspect, even if that’s not a guarantee of faithfulness. Latent representations potentially give the model more freedom, but then you have to figure out how to train that process and make sure the extra computation is actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes latent reasoning as computation in internal or continuous representations before an answer, but does not characterize it as learning algorithms in a high-dimensional representation space.

r002.rationale: It explains that language-based chain of thought writes intermediate steps as tokens that become context and serve as a scratchpad, clearly conveying reasoning scaffolded onto language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is where the intermediate computation happens. With language-based chain of thought, the model writes out intermediate steps as tokens, and then those tokens become part of the context for the next step. So it’s using language as a kind of external scratchpad.

With latent reasoning, you’re trying to do that additional computation in the model’s internal representations, without having to translate every intermediate step into a word. You might update a hidden state repeatedly and only produce language when you have an answer.

That’s appealing because language is a fairly restrictive interface. Not every useful intermediate representation has to correspond to a sentence. But there’s a trade-off: a chain of thought gives us something we can inspect, even if it isn’t necessarily a faithful explanation of the computation. With latent reasoning, it’s harder to tell what those intermediate steps are doing.

And I wouldn’t make the distinction too absolute. A model producing a chain of thought is still doing computation in its hidden states. The question is whether we require it to pass through discrete language tokens between reasoning steps, or allow it to keep working in that continuous space.

r001.rationale: The response describes latent reasoning as computation in internal representations before producing language, but does not characterize it as learning algorithms in a high-dimensional representation space.

r002.rationale: It describes language-based chain of thought as writing intermediate reasoning in language tokens that become context for subsequent steps, calling language an external scratchpad.
